sections.body: Artificial intelligence is being used across economics and investing to find patterns in data too large or too messy for older statistical methods. In macroeconomic forecasting, models now blend traditional econometrics with machine learning to process high frequency indicators, text from central bank statements, and payment data. Quantitative trading firms use machine learning to generate signals from order book data and to execute trades with less market impact. Private equity teams use AI to screen companies, parse financial statements, and flag deals earlier. Credit desks use it to score borrowers and monitor default risk in near real time. Portfolio managers use it to estimate risk and rebalance, and analysts use language models to read earnings calls, filings, and news at scale.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Forecasting has improved at short horizons and in data rich settings, but long horizon predictions remain unreliable and models struggle when the economy shifts into a regime they have not seen. Quantitative trading is mature in execution and short term signal generation, yet crowded strategies decay and the best results stay private. Credit scoring is widely deployed, but explainability and fairness requirements limit how far black box models can go in regulated lending. Portfolio construction with AI is common for risk estimation, less so for return prediction. Language models read sentiment well enough to be useful, but they still miss sarcasm, hedging, and context. Governance and fiduciary questions are the least settled, with rules on disclosure, suitability, and liability still forming.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section is built as a sequence from the broad economy down to specific markets and then to the rules over all of it. Macroeconomic Econometrics covers the forecasting end, where AI meets national accounts and central bank watching. Quantitative Trading and Fixed Income and Credit Risk show the two largest live deployments, one in liquid public markets and one in lending and bond pricing. Private Equity and Deal Sourcing and Portfolio Construction sit on the investment side, one for finding and valuing private companies, one for assembling and weighting holdings. Reading the Market's Language and Alternative Data cover the inputs, text and non traditional data sources that feed the models. Agent Workflows in Finance and Crypto Markets and Decentralised Finance cover newer territory, autonomous tool use and markets that run on blockchains. Governance and Fiduciary Risk closes the section by asking who is accountable when these systems make or inform financial decisions.
